subtype: Approach: asks an adult when the problem is unsafe or too big [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Aparna, and I was at Deepika's house when it happened. We were in the garden looking for a lost ball when Deepika went very still. "Snake," Deepika whispered. It was long and brown, near the water tap.
I wanted to look closer, but Deepika pulled me back. "Too big for us. Papa will know what to do." Deepika ran inside and came back with Papa, who told us to stand on the veranda. He called a person who helps with snakes, and we watched from the steps until the helper came.
Deepika's hands shook a little, but Deepika kept saying, "We didn't touch it."

qa.a: The snake was long and brown, near the water tap in the garden.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when standing very still in the garden?
qa.a: Deepika felt frightened, seen in the whisper and shaking hands, but also careful about staying safe.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Calling Papa worked, because the snake was too big for the children and an adult could call a person who helps with snakes.

qa.q: What was it like for Aparna to be pulled back?
qa.a: Aparna wanted to look closer, so may have felt curious and a little held back, but stayed safe on the veranda steps.

grounding: A child who finds a snake in the garden calls Papa and does not try to deal with it alone.

subtype: Approach: asks an adult when the problem is unsafe or too big [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: In school, the nature club talked about snakes. The teacher said, "If you see one, keep away and call an adult. Never try to catch it."

Thursday: Binita was watering the plants when she saw a long brown snake near the tulsi pot. Her heart thumped. She thought, "I could throw a stone. No. I don't know if it's dangerous. This is too big for me." She stepped back slowly, called her friend Jahnavi away from the garden gate, and ran inside. "Papa! There's a snake near the tulsi!" Papa came at once, kept everyone back, and called the snake rescuer.

Friday: The rescuer had taken it away safely. Binita told the nature club what she did. The teacher nodded. "Exactly right."

qa.q: Where did Binita see the snake?
What was Binita thinking when her heart thumped?
qa.a: She was scared and knew the situation was too big for her, so she chose to get an adult instead of throwing a stone.
Stepping back and calling Papa, because a snake could be dangerous and an adult could call the right help.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt being called away from the gate?
qa.a: Jahnavi was probably surprised, then relieved that Binita kept her safe.

grounding: A girl who finds a snake in the garden does not deal with it herself but calls her father, since it needs an adult.

subtype: Approach: asks an adult when the problem is unsafe or too big [Thinking]
passage: Sudha, come here. I'll tell you why your Uma Nani still checks the garden before walking barefoot. When I was nine, I was picking guavas behind our house when I saw a snake curled under the tree, as thick as my wrist. I wanted to be brave. My brother would have poked it with a stick. But I thought, "I don't know this snake. If I'm wrong, I can't undo it. This is a grown-up problem." So I backed away, very slowly, and ran for my father. He came with a long bamboo pole and sent everyone inside. Then he called the old man from the next village who knew snakes. It was a cobra. I've never forgotten how right it felt to call for help.

qa.q: How old was Uma when she saw the snake?
What was young Uma feeling as she backed away?
qa.a: She was frightened but clear-headed, knowing she didn't understand this snake and that it was a grown-up problem.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why was it right?
qa.a: Choosing to back away and call her father instead of being brave alone, because a mistake with a snake couldn't be undone.

qa.q: How might Uma's father have felt when she came running?
qa.a: He was probably alarmed but proud she had come straight to him instead of trying it herself.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a girl, finding a snake and calling her father instead of dealing with it, since it needed an adult.
